analysis.one_liner: Requires presidents to divest conflicting financial interests, disclose tax returns, and recuse appointees from matters involving them.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by 23 Democratic senators, was referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the President and Vice President to fully disclose their finances and three years of tax returns within 30 days of taking office, and to sell off or place in a blind trust any assets that could conflict with their official duties — rules that already apply to other federal employees. It would extend the same requirements to a president's spouse and minor children, require federal appointees to step aside from matters involving the president's own businesses, and make it a crime under the same statute that bars members of Congress from federal contracts. Violations could be challenged in court by the Justice Department, state attorneys general, or affected citizens.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would for the first time be able to see a president's tax returns and know whether the president's family financial holdings overlap with government decisions. It also protects federal employees and agencies, which would be required to recuse from matters involving the president's personal interests, and state governments, whose attorneys general gain standing to enforce compliance.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the President, Vice President, their spouses, and minor children to divest any financial interest that would pose a conflict of interest — either selling it or moving it to a qualified blind trust whose trustee must sell the asset and reinvest in diversified, conflict-free funds [S2, S3].

Requires the President and Vice President to file a detailed financial disclosure, including three most recent years of tax returns and any returns under IRS audit, within 30 days of taking office [S2, S3].

Makes presidential and major-party presidential candidates' tax returns public through the Office of Government Ethics or Federal Election Commission, with a fallback letting those agencies obtain the returns from the Treasury if the candidate does not file them [S3].

Requires any presidential appointee to recuse from specific matters in which the president, the president's spouse, or an entity in which either holds a substantial interest is a party, with career staff stepping in and criminal penalties for willful violations [S3].
Amends the federal conflicts law so that the President and Vice President — like members of Congress — are barred from being a party to federal contracts, closing a gap in 18 U.S.C. 431 [S3].

Gives the Justice Department, any state attorney general, or any aggrieved person the power to sue to enforce divestiture, and directs the Office of Government Ethics to report annually to Congress on whether the president is complying [S2, S3].
States the sense of Congress that a president's violation of these rules would be a high crime or misdemeanor — the constitutional standard for impeachment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Presidents, vice presidents, and their immediate families holding business or investment assets that could conflict with official duties: they would have to sell those assets or place them in blind trusts, submit to public tax return disclosure, and face potential lawsuits over compliance. A sitting president would have had 30 days after enactment to comply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Presidents and families with business holdings

drawbacks.text: Allowing 'any person aggrieved' to sue over divestiture violations invites waves of politically motivated litigation against a sitting president, and courts would be pushed into overseeing how and when presidential assets are sold [S3].

The bill itself acknowledges constitutional risk: it includes a rule of construction stating nothing should be read to violate the Constitution and a severability clause, reflecting serious questions about whether Congress can force a sitting president to sell personal assets or compel disclosure of tax returns [S3].

Forced divestiture could require selling assets on short notice, and although the bill directs courts to ensure a fair-market return for liquidated assets, complex family businesses could be hard to value or unwind [S3].
The sense-of-Congress provision declaring violations an impeachable offense is symbolic and does not itself change enforcement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and structural: it would have applied to the presidency the same conflict-of-interest rules every other federal employee already lives under, plus public tax disclosure, closing a gap that has repeatedly let a president's family businesses overlap with government power. The costs are mostly litigation risk and constitutional uncertainty, which the bill tries to manage with severability and fair-market protections but cannot fully eliminate. On balance, a strong transparency measure whose main weakness is enforceability against a resistant officeholder.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the same day, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Presidential Conflicts of Interest Act on May 9, 2023, with 22 Democratic cosponsors signing on at introduction [S3, S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs — the standard first step for a government-operations bill [S5].
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history through the end of the 118th Congress in January 2025 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting and future presidents with large personal or family financial holdings are better off: no divestiture requirement, no mandatory tax return disclosure, and no citizen or state enforcement mechanism was ever enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Presidents with large private financial holdings

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 9, 2023 and assembled 22 Democratic cosponsors at introduction

for.name: 22 Democratic senators (Murphy, Stabenow, Feinstein, Casey, Markey, Van Hollen, Blumenthal, Duckworth, Merkley, Brown, Booker, Bennet, Murray, Wyden, Cardin, Hirono, Padilla, Coons, Klobuchar, Lujan, Gillibrand, Smith)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it a full one-fifth of the Senate Democratic caucus in support

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remaining 20 months of the Congress

against.name: Senate Republican Conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and it never advanced to the floor where it could have been debated

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no one ever had to cast one; support was entirely Democratic — 23 of 23 sponsors and cosponsors — with no Republican signers, and the bill died in committee without recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Presidents, vice presidents, and their family business holdings
industries.note: The bill targets the one group of officeholders currently exempt from federal conflict-of-interest and financial-disclosure rules. Its divestiture, tax-return, and recusal requirements directly curb the ability of a president's family businesses to benefit from or overlap with government decisions, which is why the concentrated interest here is the officeholders themselves rather than a commercial industry.

industries.industry: Office of Government Ethics and federal ethics enforcement
industries.note: The bill would hand OGE new authority: setting divestiture criteria by regulation, auditing presidential finances annually, obtaining tax returns from Treasury, and publishing them. This would turn OGE from an advisory body into an enforcement agency over the presidency.
The bill gives any state attorney general standing to sue a noncompliant president in federal court, adding state-level prosecutors as independent watchdogs over presidential conflicts.
